Content: The Sea of Japan (northern and western) coast has fewer good natural ports compared to the Pacific side, in large part due to the region’s unique geological activity. Author: @Shiroskybase
Content:
As a resident of "Empty part of Japan " I felt this video is focused on how the "Taiheiyo belt" is good for industry and trade. But until the 19th century"Empty part of Japan" was not empty.

In 1880 , according to statistics by the Japanese government , the prefecture that had the largest population was Ishikawa perf (includes a part of modern Toyama and Fukui pref.) and the second largest was Niigata pref. Both of these prefectures are located on the coast side of the Sea of Japan. 
Most of the Japanese population was farmers so there were many people who live in the place where it is good for growing rice.

The capital of Japan had been Kyoto  for 1000 years and people in modern Tohoku and Hokkaido were gradually assimilated into people in "Taiheiyo belt". 
After the Meiji restoration Tokyo became the capital of Japan then concentration to the capital started.
For these historical reasons, the outside of Japan became relatively empty.

Author: @Aquapatinth
Content:
It’s great that you refer to this area as the Taiheiyō Belt — it’s more widely recognized and avoids the confusion that sometimes comes with Tōkaidō Corridor. The word Tōkaidō literally means “eastern sea route,” and it was one of the five major roads you mentioned at 15:30. This name was later reused for the Tōkaidō Shinkansen.

Regarding the high-speed rail section at 03:20 you used a route graphic from Tokyo to Fukuyama, but that’s not the full line. The Tōkaidō Shinkansen runs from Tokyo to Osaka, while the San’yō Shinkansen continues from Osaka through cities like Fukuyama and ends at Fukuoka (Hakata Station). Mentioning the full Tokyo–Osaka–Fukuoka route helps show that Japan has built a continuous high-speed rail backbone running across the entire Taiheiyō Belt, which may give your audience a clearer picture.

Author: @Tinil0
Content:
Also, forget Minneapolis, Aomori also gets damn near 3 times as much snow as Syracuse, the snowiest major city in the lower 48.  Syracuse, which has a reputation as being a winter hellscape of unending snow..."only" gets around 112 to 124 inches a year, while Aomori is around 312 inches.  This better compares to Valdez, Alaska, the snowiest city in North America, which gets up to 330 inches a year.  And of course, that's a "city" with about 4k people that you have likely never heard of unless you live in Alaska or know trivia, instead of the ~265k in Aomori.  It's truly crazy how much snow they get.  Even freaking Sapporo only gets around 190 inches a year!

(The famously snowy places in Canada, for anyone curious, are usually listed as St. John's and Saguenay, but both are only around 130 inches a year, slightly higher than Syracuse but not by a ton).
